title: Effect of Genetic Differences in Omeprazole Metabolism on Cure Rates for Helicobacter pylori Infection and Peptic Ulcer
source: Takahisa Furuta, Kyoichi Ohashi, Takashi Kamata, Misako Takashima, Kazuhiro Kosuge, Tsunehisa Kawasaki, Hiroyuki Hanai, Takahiro Kubota, Takashi Ishizaki and Eizo Kaneko. Annals of Internal Medicine 1998;129(12):1027–1030 (15 December 1998), Brief Communications
lecture: Introduced Thu 10/22 (Pharmacogenomic Examples: CYP2C19 and proton pump inhibitors); discussed in detail Mon 10/26.
about: This reading is a short 1998 research paper from the Annals of Internal Medicine that asked whether a patient's CYP2C19 genotype, the gene for the liver enzyme that clears omeprazole, predicts whether omeprazole plus amoxicillin cures Helicobacter pylori infection and heals a peptic ulcer. It matters for Exam 4 because Dr. Smith listed two things from it: the functional significance of the three genotype groups for the H. pylori cure rate, and the four ways that higher omeprazole concentrations in poor metabolizers improved patient outcomes. The study followed 62 Japanese patients with peptic ulcer (33 gastric, 29 duodenal) and H. pylori infection, all treated with dual therapy: omeprazole 20 mg once daily for 8 weeks (gastric ulcer) or 6 weeks (duodenal ulcer) plus amoxicillin 500 mg four times daily for the first 2 weeks (p. 1027). Patients were genotyped for two mutated alleles, CYP2C19m1 in exon 5 and CYP2C19m2 in exon 4, and grouped as no mutation (group 1, n = 28), one mutation (group 2, n = 25) or two mutations (group 3, n = 9), corresponding to rapid-extensive, intermediate-extensive and poor-metabolizer phenotypes (p. 1028). Cure rates for H. pylori infection were 28.6%, 60% and 100% in the rapid-, intermediate- and poor-metabolizer groups, and ulcer healing rates were roughly parallel (abstract; Table 2). The Discussion gives four reasons for the higher cure rate in poor metabolizers and notes the poor-metabolizer genotype is 3% to 5% in white U.S. or European populations versus 18% to 23% in Japanese persons (p. 1029). The authors state the limitations that plasma omeprazole levels were not measured and the sample was small (p. 1029).

read_for: 1. Functional significance, group 1 (Table 1, Table 2, p. 1028-1029): wild-type/wild-type (her labels *1/*1), two working copies of CYP2C19, the rapid-extensive metabolizer; relative omeprazole AUC 1; H. pylori cured in 28.6% (8 of 28).
2. Functional significance, group 2: wild-type/m1 or wild-type/m2 (*1/*2 or *1/*3), one working copy, the intermediate-extensive metabolizer; relative AUC 3.7; cured in 60.0% (15 of 25).

3. Functional significance, group 3: m1/m2 or m1/m1 (*2/*3 or *2/*2), no working copy, the poor metabolizer; relative AUC 20; cured in 100% (9 of 9). The cure rate was highest in group 3, intermediate in group 2 and lowest in group 1, P < 0.001 (Table 2).

4. What the mutations are (Table 1 footnote; Methods, p. 1028): CYP2C19m1 is a mutation in exon 5 and CYP2C19m2 a mutation in exon 4, typed by PCR restriction fragment length polymorphism. Her 10/26 addition: m1 is *2, m2 is *3, each a SNP creating a premature stop codon, so the protein is too short to work.

5. Ulcer healing (abstract; Results, pp. 1028-1029): healing of gastric and duodenal ulcer was roughly parallel with the cure rates, and every ulcer healed in patients whose H. pylori infection was cured; the Discussion credits both the higher cure rate and the stronger acid inhibition in poor metabolizers.

6. Way 1 of 4 (Discussion, p. 1029, 'First'): omeprazole's plasma concentration-time curve is markedly increased in poor metabolizers, so high intragastric pH lasts longer than in extensive metabolizers.
7. Way 2 of 4 ('Second'): amoxicillin is unstable and less active at low pH, so raising intragastric pH toward neutral increases the amount of active antibiotic.

8. Way 3 of 4 ('Third'): omeprazole has been reported to increase amoxicillin concentrations in gastric juice, so amoxicillin stays in the stomach longer at levels above its minimum inhibitory concentration. (She said it is amoxicillin, not omeprazole, that ends up higher in the gastric juice.)
9. Way 4 of 4 ('Finally'): omeprazole itself has reported anti-H. pylori activity, presumably enhanced in poor metabolizers. She summarized the first three in class; the fourth is in the paper only.

10. Why it does not transfer to the United States on its face (Discussion, p. 1029): the poor-metabolizer genotype is 3% to 5% in white U.S. or European populations versus 18% to 23% in Japanese persons; with genotyping the same genotype is expected to respond the same way.
beyond_lecture: Results, p. 1028: adherence to the regimen (100% in 43 patients, about 90% in 18, about 75% in 1) and eradication by adherence level (58%, 33%, 100%).

Discussion, p. 1029: Bayerdorffer and associates' high-dose dual therapy (omeprazole 40 mg three times daily plus amoxicillin 750 mg three times daily, 91% cure in white persons) and the suggestion that at least 120 mg of omeprazole a day may be needed in extensive metabolizers.

Discussion, pp. 1029-1030: the cost of genotyping and of larger omeprazole doses against the savings from avoiding a second antibiotic; the clinical usefulness and cost-effectiveness of genotyping remain to be determined.

Methods, p. 1028: how cure was judged (culture, histology, rapid urease test, 13C-urea breath test and PCR; a positive result on any test meant failure) and the statistics (one-way ANOVA, Fisher exact test).
Results, p. 1028: no clinically undesirable signs or symptoms attributable to the dual therapy were recognized.

terms.chapter_definition: The genetically determined liver enzyme that metabolizes omeprazole; S-mephenytoin 4'-hydroxylase is the paper's older name for it (p. 1027).

A person whose CYP2C19 phenotype or genotype gives little or no enzyme activity; in them the area under the plasma concentration-time curve of omeprazole is markedly increased, so the clinical effect of omeprazole should be greater (p. 1027).

The area under the plasma concentration-time curve, the paper's measure of how much omeprazole is in circulation; the relative mean AUC in rapid, intermediate and poor metabolizers has been reported as 1:3.7:20 (p. 1028).
The two mutated alleles the study genotyped: m1 is a mutation in exon 5 and m2 a mutation in exon 4 of the gene; wt is the wild-type, working allele (Table 1 footnote).
Wild-type/wild-type patients (n = 28), whose phenotype is the rapid-extensive metabolizer: full enzyme activity (p. 1028).
Wild-type/m1 or wild-type/m2 patients (n = 25), the intermediate-extensive metabolizer: one working allele (p. 1028).
m1/m2 or m1/m1 patients (n = 9), the poor metabolizer: no working allele (p. 1028).
Omeprazole plus one antibiotic, amoxicillin; it gives somewhat lower cure rates than triple therapy but avoids the problems of clarithromycin and metronidazole (p. 1027).
A proton-pump inhibitor, amoxicillin, and clarithromycin or metronidazole; H. pylori resistance to the latter two drugs has been reported (p. 1027).
The antibiotic level needed to stop the bacterium; the third reason says amoxicillin stays in the stomach longer at levels exceeding it when omeprazole is co-administered (p. 1029).
Judged one month after treatment by culture, histology, rapid urease testing, 13C-urea breath testing and PCR; a positive result on any test counted as failure (p. 1028).

listen: This reading is the brief communication Effect of Genetic Differences in Omeprazole Metabolism on Cure Rates for Helicobacter pylori Infection and Peptic Ulcer, by Takahisa Furuta and colleagues, in the Annals of Internal Medicine, December nineteen ninety eight. It is a prospective cohort study of sixty two Japanese patients with gastric or duodenal ulcer and Helicobacter pylori infection. Every patient received dual therapy: omeprazole twenty milligrams once daily, for eight weeks for gastric ulcer or six weeks for duodenal ulcer, plus amoxicillin five hundred milligrams four times daily for the first two weeks. Omeprazole is metabolized in the liver by sip two C nineteen. The authors genotyped two mutated alleles, m one in exon five and m two in exon four, and grouped patients by the number of mutations. Group one had no mutation and corresponds to rapid extensive metabolizers. Group two had one mutation and corresponds to intermediate extensive metabolizers. Group three had two mutations and corresponds to poor metabolizers. The relative mean area under the curve for omeprazole in these three groups has been reported as one to three point seven to twenty. Cure rates for the infection were twenty eight point six percent, sixty percent, and one hundred percent in the rapid, intermediate and poor metabolizer groups. Ulcer healing rates were roughly parallel with the cure rates. The authors give four reasons. Poor metabolizers have more omeprazole in circulation, so high intragastric pH lasts longer. Amoxicillin is unstable and less active at low pH. Omeprazole has been reported to increase amoxicillin concentrations in gastric juice. And omeprazole itself has been reported to have activity against Helicobacter pylori. The poor metabolizer genotype is found in three to five percent of white United States or European populations and eighteen to twenty three percent of Japanese persons. The limitations they state: they did not measure plasma omeprazole levels, and the sample was small. In class on October twenty second, she introduced it as a very interesting study done in a Japanese population, about two C nineteen. She said that poor metabolizers on proton pump inhibitors had better cure rates, because the drug stays in the body and proton pump inhibitors have a very wide therapeutic index. On October twenty sixth she walked through the paper: group three, with no active enzyme, had the best cure rate; star two and star three are nonfunctional because of a premature stop codon; the discussion's first, second and third points are that omeprazole stays high so gastric pH is higher, amoxicillin is more stable at the higher pH, and more amoxicillin reaches the gastric juice where H. pylori is; and the result cannot be generalized to the United States on its face, but could be with genotyping. For the exam she listed the functional significance of the genotypes for the cure rate and the four ways elevated P P I concentrations improved outcomes. The figure she showed as that paper's data used lansoprazole and plotted area under the curve, stomach pH and cure rate. The nineteen ninety eight paper used omeprazole and did not measure plasma drug levels.
